titolo: Amodei's Claude 'Solved' Riemann. Nobody Knows Why It Works
angolo: Day 3: The code is machine-certified, but no human can yet explain why it works, and the credit and prize questions are just opening.
descrizione: Amodei's Claude 'Solved' Riemann. Nobody Knows Why It Works. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis, and the Lean and Mathlib communities have certified the proof as correct. But mathematicians say the ideas are not yet understood, a rival human claim has surfaced, and the Clay Prize clock has not started. Here is exactly what is confirmed and what is not, according to AP, Nature, Al Jazeera and Scientific American.
tag: Amodei's Claude 'Solved' Riemann. Nobody Knows Why It Works

scene.testo: A computer has checked every step of a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and independent mathematicians say it compiles without issues.
Lean and Mathlib communities say it is correct.
But a leading mathematician says nobody yet understands what it shows.
Did Anthropic's Claude just help solve math's greatest mystery, and who actually understands the answer?
It started on a Friday, one day after Anthropic's Nasdaq debut.
Mathematician Levent Alpöge posted a four-page note on his website.
Its first line made headlines in the math world.
He wrote what he believed he had found.

visivo.testo: He wrote what he believed he had found.

citazione.testo: I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis

scene.testo: The Riemann hypothesis dates to 1859 and concerns prime numbers.
It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems listed by the Clay Mathematics Institute.
Each carries a one million dollar prize, according to the Clay Mathematics Institute.
Alpöge also claimed the method resolves the generalized version.
In a moment: the number that makes this proof unusual.
He did not publish a conventional paper.
He released the argument in Lean, a proof assistant that checks logic step by step.
According to Science magazine, that was about seventeen million lines of code.
Alpöge said he messaged his boss first.
Alpöge said the discovery came late Sunday night.
He messaged CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," NPR reported.
The company was about to make major news with its stock debut.
Anthropic priced its shares at eighty-three dollars on November eighteenth, according to CBS News and other outlets.
Who is the man whose company is at the center of this story?
Anthropic's shares opened at one hundred eleven dollars and fifty cents, CBS News reported.
The IPO raised about eighty-one billion dollars, a record, according to NPR and CNN.
Now, the hard part. Was the proof really checked?
MIT's Andrew Sutherland compiled the code on his own computers.
It compiled without issues, and Sutherland said it was independently rechecked by the Lean kernel using only the three standard axioms.
Sutherland told Scientific American the chance anything is fishy is approximately zero.

citazione.testo: Honestly the chance that anything is fishy here is approximately zero.

scene.testo: On November twenty-first, the Lean FRO and Mathlib communities issued a joint statement, according to reports.
They said they have full confidence the proof is correct.

visivo.testo: They said they have full confidence the proof is correct.

scene.testo: Dozens of people independently compiled the code, according to reports on that joint statement.
So is the case closed? Not quite.
Here is where the story turns.
Imperial College's Kevin Buzzard said nobody yet understands what the proof actually shows.
Compiling only means each step is valid in Lean; mathematicians say humans must still confirm the statement is right and understand the ideas.
Oxford's James Maynard said he suspects the proof will turn out to be correct.
Yet Nature reported that Maynard described the proof as now existing in the form of incomprehensible code.
Rutgers professor Alex Kontorovich described an out-of-body experience, according to NPR.
A natural-language proof that humans can read has yet to be published.

visivo.testo: A natural-language proof that humans can read has yet to be published.

scene.testo: Another question hangs over the work: does the Lean statement match the real theorem?
Buzzard said the first question to ask is whether the statement in the Lean code corresponds to the actual theorem.
The Lean and Mathlib statement says two independent tools confirmed the statements match, according to reports.
Then came a second claim on the same day.
Scientific American reported a second claim, this one by a human, that had not been verified.
Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society, posted about it on his blog.
He said Stanford's Alessandro Masullo had written the proof, all human, with no AI, according to the post.
Scientific American's Brian Conrad said the work is undergoing major revision.
Meanwhile, a debate erupted over who deserves the credit.
Alpöge himself wrote that Claude far outpaced him near the finish line, according to Al Jazeera.
One mathematician told Al Jazeera others with similar access to frontier AI models had not found a proof.
Nature quoted number theorist Andrew Granville criticizing the timing.
He said a clearer write-up should have come before the announcement.
Nature said the announcement came just days after Anthropic's IPO.
As of Friday morning, Scientific American reported Anthropic had issued no public statement on the claim.
Back in August, Anthropic reported Claude had raised a known bound on the share of zeta zeros on the line, but not proved the full hypothesis.
Anthropic reported it had raised a known bound from forty-one point six to sixty-seven point two percent.
Three months later, Alpöge claimed a full proof.
Meanwhile on Wall Street, shares fell about 8.5 percent on day two, closing at $88.91, per market reports.
Day one closed at ninety-seven dollars seventeen, up seventeen percent from the offer, CBS News reported.
So can the prize be claimed? Here is the catch, according to the Clay Institute's rules.
The Clay Institute's rules require publication in a qualifying outlet.
Then at least two years must pass after publication.
And the work must gain general acceptance in the mathematics community.
The institute does not accept direct submissions.
What happens next? Al Jazeera reports mathematicians say it may take weeks to understand.
In his note, Alpöge also said he expects the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, with more time.
For now, here is what is confirmed.
The code compiles, and the Lean and Mathlib communities say it is correct.
What is not yet confirmed: the underlying ideas, peer review, and the prize.
The machine has checked the code. Now the humans must understand it.
The story is still moving. Subscribe, so you see what comes next.
